title: Chapter 7: The Rule as Written
blurb: A copper ring in the reed and a Court inquiry put the Seven on trial, and the Clerk has a question of her own for Sorrel.

blocks.text: The reed at the Hobsmere reed-line had gone the colour of a fox in the thin winter sun, and a party of long-tailed tits was working along it in little bursts of grey and pink, when Wilfred Cobbing put his hand down among the stems beside his eel traps and brought up a ring of copper. It was green at the edges, cold, and wet from the mere. He held it out to Joan on his flat palm as though it might bite.
Copper inside the reed-line, on anyone but a ringed player, is Shade-planting.
Joan took it from him and folded it into her handkerchief and put it in her coat pocket, and for a long while none of us said anything at all.

It was Tuesday, two days before the Court would sit. On Monday night there had been one charge against the Seven, the one in the cream envelope: that holding the point bird at Wenlode was outside the rules. Now there were two, and the second lay in Joan's coat pocket, wrapped in a handkerchief.
"May I see it?" I asked.

I turned it under my loft glass. It was a closed band, a wrist's width, and where the stamp should have been there was only a crust of green and a dent, as if a boot or a cart wheel had pressed it into the silt. I could not read a numeral on it, or a number. I held it the way I would hold a bird's leg, lightly, and I was sorry for it, which is a strange thing to feel for copper.

"Been in there a good while, by the green," Wilfred said. He was a small brown man with eel-slime to the elbow and a voice like a gate. "I've had my hands in that reed forty year. Could've come off any wrist, any match. Hamish's day. Before Hamish."
"Could have," Joan said. "Copper doesn't grow in reed, though, does it?"

Out on the mere a pair of great crested grebes were facing each other with their crests up, shaking their heads, and the water between them was the pale clean blue of a duck's egg. I watched them because I did not want to watch Joan's face. It was the water Hamish had walked into. It was the water I had nearly walked into. And somebody, some winter, some day, had let a ring fall into the reed beside it, or had put it there.
"If anyone else finds that," I said, "they will say we planted it."
"So nobody else finds it, do they?" Joan said. "We take it to Wenlode on Thursday and put it on the Court's table ourselves, before anyone can find it for us. That's what we do, isn't it?"
"Yes," I said.
"Yes," said Wilfred, and went back to his traps, and did not mend a single one all morning.

Walking home along the causeway, with a skein of geese going over low toward the washes, I did not think of the points. I thought of the Cutters' card taken down off the draw board at the Loft, and Wilfred's eel-cart standing at the soft end of the causeway on a Saturday with nothing to carry.

On Thursday we took the early train, Joan and Wilfred and I, through a white frost that lay on every field like flour on a board. Rooks were up out of the shelter belts in their hundreds, going out to the ploughland, and lapwings stood in the furrows all facing one way into the wind. Joan kept her hand on her coat pocket the whole journey.

The long room of the Ringing House smelled of beeswax and coal smoke. The framed charter hung on the end wall, and I read the line again while we waited, because I could not stop myself: The Long Final stands open until the first ring is opened.

Augusta Stannard sat beneath it at the centre of a long table, a tall woman in dark grey, with white hair drawn back very smooth and reading spectacles on a ribbon. The clerk who had stamped my ring sat at the end with a ledger. Wenlode Sluice's secretary, a heavy man in a velvet-collared coat, had a chair of his own; their Wing stood behind him in his oilskin, looking at his boots. Dorcas Ely sat apart with a leather case on her knees. And on the bench by the window, in grey and gold, sat Fallowby Wardens' secretary, and beside him Clemency Stannard, very straight, with her gloves in her lap.

"The Court sits," said Augusta, "upon the representation of Wenlode Sluice, entered at this House in the week of the fifteenth match of the two hundred and third season, flown at the Sluice Reedbed. In the middle of a season the Court may rule only whether a thing broke the rules as written. A result is voided only for a proven foul."
Joan was on her feet before the Wenlode man.

"Before Wenlode speak, Clerk, will the Court take this from us?" She unfolded the handkerchief on the table. "Found on Tuesday in our own reed at Hobsmere by our chairman. You'd rather have it from us than from anyone else, wouldn't you?"

Augusta looked at the ring a long moment without touching it. "The Court will enter it," she said, "as a second question: whether the holding at Wenlode was made with copper on anyone but a ringed player."

The Wenlode secretary spoke first to the holding. His Tacker's shade, he said, had been drawn into a Hobsmere cluster and used as if it were Hobsmere's own. A side owns six shades. To make a seventh out of an opponent's was Shade-planting by another name.

Joan answered him with questions, each already answered. "Was your Tacker ringed at the Ringing? He was. Did your own Wing close that ring on him? He did. Did your Wing raise that shade? He did. So whose copper was it, and on whose wrist, and where's the planting in that, back-flow and all?"
Then Clemency Stannard rose, and the Fallowby secretary looked up at her, surprised.

"If the Clerk will allow Fallowby Wardens a word on the wording," she said, low and very clear. Augusta inclined her head. Clemency opened no book; she had the words already. "'Holding needs seven shades nearer the bird than any real bird, which means seven ringed people within about a pace of each other on the ground. A side owns only six shades, so a seventh must be an opponent's raised shade standing in the cluster, or a handed ring.'" "The rule names the thing Hobsmere Cutters did, Clerk, and permits it. I should rather meet the Seven on a Reedbed than be spared it in this room." She sat down and folded her hands on her gloves, and did not look at me.
I understood her then, or thought I did. She did not want it taken from me. She wanted to beat it.
The second question was harder, because a ring is a thing you can put on a table, and a thread is not.
"A club that keeps copper in its own reed," said the Wenlode secretary, "has had a use for copper in reed. A ringed body can lie flat in a reedbed, Clerk. Our sluice reed would hide a cow."
Augusta turned her spectacles toward me. "Miss Tansley. You were Wing. Tell the Court what you saw."
So I told them slowly, from the birds, the only way I know.

I told them that in High Flight, after the gale had torn my herding away, I raised only my own shade at eight minutes past four, alone at the height the point birds were running downwind. I told them that I read the point bird's seven then, as a Wing can, the fine threads of its attention going out from it like the spokes of a wheel, to its fellows in the flock, to Wenlode's shades, which their Wing had brought up to my height, and to my own shade, and that not one went down toward the reed-line. I told them that in the Gloaming, at Wenlode's Roost mouth, its seven were six Hobsmere shades over Joan and Mercy and Abel and Rhys and Lucas and me, and the shade of the Tacker who had followed Joan into the cluster. Seven threads, all on shades I could name by the copper on their legs. Not one to the reed.

"A person can lie down in a reedbed," I said, "but a shade cannot. It flies at the ceiling over whoever wears the copper. If anyone had been lying in the sluice reed with a ring on, there would have been a bird-shape over the sluice reed for every sighted person on the field to see."
"Was there anything else in the point bird's seven?" Augusta asked.

"No," I said, which was true. The extra bird had been eighth. It had flown at my shade's wingtip, close enough to count and choosing not to be, and she had asked me about the seven. I sat down. I understood, sitting down, that I was glad nobody had asked me about the eighth, and I did not like knowing that about myself.

Dorcas Ely was sworn. She opened her case and read from her sheet in her flat, careful counter's voice: Hobsmere's six numbers, twenty-three to twenty-seven and seventy-one, entered against the settle, and one number of Wenlode's. No other.
"Did you see a shade over the reed-line, Miss Ely, at any time in that match?"
"No, Clerk. Not at any time. Every shade I saw on that point bird is on my sheet." She did not look at me. She had not looked at me at the Ringing either.

Augusta took off her spectacles. "The ring was found at Hobsmere. The match was flown at Wenlode. The Court has no proof that this copper was ever worn by anyone, at either place, or when it came into the reed. The second question is dismissed for want of proof. The ring will go to the Circuit Loft." The clerk wrote. Joan's handkerchief came back across the table, empty.

Nobody said who had dropped it, or put it there. Nobody could. I thought of the grebes on the clean blue water, and of a ring lying green among the stems for a season or for a week, and I knew I would never be told which.
The Fallowby secretary stood up then, a thin man with a grey-and-gold scarf wound twice round his neck, and he spoke pleasantly, as if asking after the weather.
"One more matter, Clerk, since the Court is sitting. It is said about the Circuit that Hobsmere's new Wing counts birds that are not there. Is such a Wing fit to be registered?"
Clemency Stannard sat beside him with her hands folded on her gloves and said nothing at all.

The room went quiet in a way I felt on my skin, the way you feel the cold come off the mere at dusk before you see the mist rise. I looked at the tall window. Beyond it the town fell away down its hill in slate roofs, white with frost on their north faces and wet and dark on their south, all the way to the river, and the river was the colour of pewter, and a heron was going over it very slowly, legs trailing, toward the sluice gates. I watched it the whole way, because if I could keep the heron in the sky and the river under it, I could keep myself in my chair. I had said forty-one aloud at a reed-line, once, because it was true, and it seemed to me that everyone in this room knew it.
Joan stood up.

She did not ask anyone anything this time. She walked to the end of the table where the Court's rule book lay, opened it at the charter's registration article, and read it aloud, word for word, in the voice she uses for the drainage board.

"'A player nominated by her club before the close shall be registered, and shall not be refused nor struck save upon one of these grounds, and no other: that she is in the employ of the Circuit Loft or holds a counter's licence and has not left that post; that she has failed to take the Breath, the failure being proved in open Court upon the sworn timing of a counter or of the holder of the watch, a late call being no failure of hers; or that her club has withdrawn its nomination. No ground shall be heard but in open Court, the Clerk presiding, and the player and her club may answer it.'" She closed the book. "Our nomination stands, doesn't it, Clerk? And counting isn't on that list, is it?"
Augusta looked at Joan, and not at me.

"The article was settled in the second season," she said, "and it has not been amended since. Amendments govern play. They do not govern who may play. The question is not before the Court, and it will not come before it." She turned a page. "We proceed to the ruling."

"The Court finds that the holding of the point bird at the Sluice Reedbed, in the fifteenth match of this season, was within the rules as written. No foul is proven. The result stands: Wenlode Sluice nought, Hobsmere Cutters four."
Seventeen points. It stayed seventeen. I felt it settle in me the way a crate settles on the cart when the last bird is in.

Out in the corridor Joan sat down on a wooden bench with her hands on her knees, and for almost a minute she did not swear at all. I had never known her go so long. I sat down beside her, and after a while I put my hand over her wrist, where the withy goes on a match day, and held it there, and she let me.
"Silt," she said at last, very quietly. "Silt and sumps and the whole blessed back-flow."
"Yes," I said.
The door of the long room opened and Augusta Stannard came out, the clerk behind her. She stopped in front of our bench. She did not raise her voice; I do not think she ever has.

"Miss Pettifer. You will wish to know what the rule will be next season. From the first Ringing of the two hundred and fourth season, the Crowding amendment applies in both phases. When ringed players of both sides stand within a pace of each other, in a group of three or more, for more than five seconds, the side with more players in the group fouls. Both sides, if equal. It will be published a month before the Ringing, as is proper." She drew on her gloves, one finger at a time. "Your Seven will be a foul in a year. This season it stands."
"Then we'll use it this season, won't we," said Joan.
"I expect you will," said Augusta.

We went out to the street door, and the cold came in at us off the hill with the smell of the river on it, and rooks going over high toward their wood. Joan and Wilfred went down the steps. I was the last through, and on the threshold Augusta Stannard said my name.
I turned. She stood just inside, in the shadow of the hall, with the charter on the wall behind her.
"How many did you count, Miss Tansley?" she asked quietly.

I have let things stand before. I let my aunt call my long walk sleepwalking, and I kept my sight to myself for years. But I had never once in my life said aloud a thing that was not so. Not an hour since, I had sat in that room while it asked whether a Wing who counts forty-one is fit to fly, and the heron had gone over the river, and Joan had read the article out word for word to keep me.
"Forty," I said.
Augusta Stannard smiled at me as though that were the right answer.
